Match loose pieces to the map

Jigsaw Piece Finder

Photograph the finished puzzle and lay a grid over it. Then photograph a sheet of loose pieces and drag the grid lines until every piece sits in its own box — the grid lines you drag are what define each piece, and the app cuts each piece out of its box and matches it against every box on the map, trying it four ways round. Sheet after sheet adds up, and every piece you place is remembered on the board in step 4.

2

Photograph a sheet of pieces

Help

Lay loose pieces face-up on a plain dark sheet or tray, roughly in rows. Then drag the grid lines on the photo — side to side, up and down — until every piece sits inside its own box. Pieces that have slid a little are fine: you line the grid up to the pieces, not the other way round. The grid lines are what define each piece — the app cuts each piece straight out of its box. The counts below set how many boxes the grid has, and name the rows. This first sheet holds 20 pieces — 5 across by 4 down. When a sheet is checked, save its pieces and photograph the next one — the app keeps every sheet’s pieces together, and step 3 matches them all at once.

For a good sheet photo

  • Even light — no glare or bright spots on the pieces.
  • No shadow falling across the sheet.
  • Every piece flat and face-up, and not touching its neighbours — each piece inside its own grid box.
  • Drag each grid line until it runs between two rows or columns of pieces, so every piece sits inside one box. A piece that has slid out of line is fine — move the lines to fit it.
  • The whole sheet in the frame, photographed straight from above.

4

The pieces, cut out

Each piece is cut straight out of its grid box, in reading order — across, then down — and every cut-out is the same size, so the pieces line up in even rows. Check that each cut-out holds one whole piece. If a piece was missed or cut badly, drag the grid lines so it sits in its own box, retake the photo, and cut again.

Not confirmed yet — check each piece, then tap the green button.

Saving a sheet keeps its pieces in the pool for matching, and frees step 2 for the next sheet photo. Pieces from every saved sheet are matched together in step 3.

3

Match the pieces

Help

The app compares every cut-out piece against every box on the map — by colour and by the pattern of the picture — trying each piece at 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° and keeping the best fit. Each card shows the piece turned the way it fits — the rotation that produced its best fit. Each piece gets a Fit score out of 10, always shown with its word.

Cut the sheet in step 2 first — matching works on the cut-out pieces.

–LOCKED

Fit 8 to 10. The app is sure. Place the piece.

–SOFT

Fit 5 to 7. Probably right — worth a quick look before placing.

–CONFLICT

Two pieces want the same box. The higher score keeps it; the other piece is shown its next-best box.

–UNPLACED

Fit below 5. No box scored well enough. Take a better photo, or place it by hand.

–PLACED

Pieces put in by hand.

The map, with every match pinned

LOCKED SOFT CONFLICT — pinned at the box it wanted Other possible fit (gray square) Pin numbers are the piece numbers on the cards below. Every piece with a suggested fit is pinned, CONFLICT pieces included. UNPLACED pieces get no pin.

The puzzle so far

Every piece you mark as placed in step 3 appears here, in its box on the map, turned the way it fits — the puzzle filling in as you go. The board stays put while you add more sheets, and the list under it is the record of what is in, box by box.

A progress file holds the whole sitting: the map photo and its grid, and every piece cut so far — each with its match and whether it is placed. Save at the end of a sitting, then load the file at the next one to pick up exactly where you left off. On a desktop browser you choose the file once and later saves update that same file; on iPhone the save downloads the file, and loading means choosing it again.

A word of caution

Matching from photos is a first pass, not gospel — plain and dark pieces are genuinely hard, because several boxes look alike. That is why every score travels with its word, why plain pieces show their other possible fits as gray squares on the map instead of one answer, and why a SOFT or CONFLICT card always asks for a human glance before the piece goes in.

Help

Setting up the map

  1. Start from a photo of the finished puzzle — the completed puzzle itself, the box lid, or the poster picture.
  2. The four red dots mark the corners of the picture (not the photo). They start in the photo’s outer corners — if the picture fills the photo edge to edge, they may already be right. Drag each dot onto its corner.
  3. Set the boxes across and boxes down to match how you want the picture divided. Each box gets a name: a column letter plus a row number — A1 is top left, and with 6 across and 8 down the bottom right box is F8.
  4. Look along the grid lines: they should follow the picture evenly, with no drift at the far side. If the bottom lines sit lower than they should, a corner is off — nudge it.
  5. When the grid sits right, tap The grid sits right on the picture. Changing a corner or a count afterwards asks you to confirm again.

Photographing a sheet of pieces

  1. Lay the pieces face-up on a plain dark sheet or tray, roughly in rows and columns. They do not need to line up exactly — you drag the grid lines on the photo until every piece sits inside its own box, and the app cuts each piece straight out of its box. The grid lines are what define each piece; there is no outline reading.
  2. Keep pieces apart where you can, one piece to a box. A piece that has slid a little out of line is fine — move the grid lines to fit it.
  3. Use even light with no glare, and keep shadows — including your own — off the sheet. Dark pieces on a dark tray are the hardest to tell apart; steady, even light helps most.
  4. Hold the phone straight above the sheet and fill the frame with it; include the whole sheet, edge to edge.
  5. Set the pieces-across and pieces-down counts to match how many pieces you laid out, drag the grid lines until each piece sits in its own box — drag a line by its middle, side to side or up and down — then tap Cut out the pieces in the grid.
  6. Check the cut-outs: one whole piece each, all the same size. If a cut-out holds only part of a piece, the grid lines are off — drag them so the whole piece sits inside its box, and cut again.
  7. A puzzle takes many sheets, and this step repeats for each one. After checking a sheet’s cut-outs, tap Save these pieces & photograph another sheet — those pieces stay in the pool, step 2 frees up for the next photo, and step 3 matches every piece from every sheet together.

Matching

  1. Tap Match the pieces once the sheet is cut. The app tries every piece against every box on the map, at four rotations, comparing colour and the pattern of the picture.
  2. Every piece gets a Fit score out of 10, always with its word: LOCKED (8–10, the app is sure), SOFT (5–7, probably right — look before placing), UNPLACED (below 5, no good match).
  3. If two pieces both fit one box best, the higher score keeps the box and the other is marked CONFLICT, with its next-best box shown. A box is never given to two pieces without saying so.
  4. Plain or dark pieces look like many boxes at once. Their other possible fits appear on the card’s map as gray squares, so a person can judge between them.
  5. Changing the map grid or re-cutting the sheet clears the matching — run it again afterwards.
  6. The piece photo on each card is turned the way the piece will sit in the puzzle — the rotation that gave its best fit — so what you see is the piece as it goes in, not as it lay on the sheet.
  7. On each card the piece photo sits in the left column. Above the gold info box, every possible box for the piece is listed, best first — for example “B7 - SOFT Fit 6/10 ★” for the best fit, then “A7 - SOFT Fit 5/10” — the box, its word, the Fit score, and a gold star at the end of the best fit line only. Just above the gold info box, on the right, is a Placed checkbox — tick it when the piece is in. The comments sit in the gold box under that checkbox. The small map sits right-justified in the right column; the piece’s other possible fits appear on that map as gray squares with the piece number in gray inside — square, so they can’t be mistaken for the round best-fit pin. CONFLICT pieces are pinned on the map too, at the box they wanted — their next-best box shows as a gray square.
  8. Above the cards, one dropdown filter picks which pieces the cards show: open it and tick any mix of LOCKED, SOFT, CONFLICT, UNPLACED and Placed — or All pieces to see everything again.
  9. When you physically put a piece in, tick the Placed checkbox above the gold info box on its card. It is remembered on the board in step 4, in its box, and stays there while you add more sheets.

The board and the progress file

  1. Tick the Placed checkbox on a piece’s card in step 3 once the piece is physically in the puzzle. The piece appears on the board in step 4, in its box, turned the way it fits best, with its Fit score in the list under the board.
  2. The board is the app’s memory of what is placed, box by box. Adding more sheets does not disturb it. Changing the map grid does — the boxes move, so the board clears; a progress file saved beforehand brings the placements back with the grid they belong to.
  3. Save Progress File writes the whole sitting to one file on your computer: the map photo and grid, and every piece cut so far — each with a small picture, its match and Fit score, and whether it is placed. Keep the file with the puzzle. On a desktop browser the first save lets you choose where the file lives, and later saves update that same file; on iPhone the save downloads the file instead.
  4. Load Progress File at your next sitting puts everything back — the map and its grid, every piece with its match, and the board exactly as it was — then photograph the next sheet of pieces and carry on.
Jigsaw Piece Finder is a work in progress at Exponology. Sheets add up, placed pieces are remembered on the board, and a progress file carries them to your next sitting; scores are a first pass — check SOFT and CONFLICT cards before placing.
